title: Mpox Research | Ayel L. R. Batac
text:
\(~\)
Mpox is an infectious disease caused by the monkeypox virus, which can spread between people through close physical contact. Although the disease has been recognised in parts of Africa for decades, the multinational outbreak associated with clade IIb in 2022 marked a significant expansion in its geographical distribution. Subsequent outbreaks involving clade I have raised new questions about transmission patterns and the populations affected.
In Canada and many other countries, the 2022 outbreak disproportionately affected gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men. Recognising these patterns is important for targeted prevention, but public health responses must also account for transmission in other populations without reinforcing stigma. My research examines how emerging epidemiological evidence can inform mpox preparedness and response in Canada.


Reported differences in disease severity between mpox outbreaks do not necessarily reflect differences in the virus itself. The populations affected and their access to testing and treatment can influence which cases are detected and the outcomes recorded. Assessing emerging evidence on the transmission and clinical characteristics of mpox clades therefore requires careful interpretation, particularly when considering whether findings from one outbreak can inform public health responses in another setting.
Similar challenges arise when interpreting surveillance data. Declining numbers of reported mpox cases do not necessarily mean that transmission has ended, especially when testing access or reporting practices have changed. Continued case reporting can help public health authorities detect renewed transmission and changes in the populations affected. Examining these trends alongside emerging evidence on viral clades can inform public health risk assessment and decisions about surveillance as outbreak conditions evolve.




Public health professionals need access to reliable information as evidence about mpox continues to develop. Changes in epidemiological understanding can have practical implications for assessing suspected infections and determining appropriate public health responses.


Through my work at National Collaborating Centre for Infectious Diseases ↗, I synthesised available evidence and public health guidance into a resource intended for Canadian practitioners. The aim was to make emerging research accessible and relevant to public health decisions, particularly where recommendations must account for uncertainty in the available evidence.

Differences between mpox outbreaks, coupled with uncertainty in surveillance data, can complicate decisions about public health responses. By synthesising emerging evidence and examining its implications for practice, my work aims to contribute to mpox preparedness and control by:

Supporting public health risk assessment through evidence on emerging viral clades and changing transmission patterns.

Informing the interpretation of surveillance trends and decisions about continued case reporting.
Making emerging epidemiological and clinical evidence more accessible to public health professionals.
Supporting risk communication that reflects the circumstances of affected populations without reinforcing stigma.

title: How I Found My Way to Public Health | Ayel L. R. Batac
text:
How I Found My Way to Public Health
May 7, 2025
\(~\)
When I started studying molecular biology as an undergraduate, I had a fairly ambitious goal. I wanted to help cure cancer.
I was fascinated by the human body and how much was happening at a level we couldn’t see. The more I learned about molecular processes, the more interested I became in what happens when they go wrong. Cancer had affected several members of my family, and I had lost relatives to it. I thought that if I could understand disease at its most fundamental level, I might one day contribute to finding a cure.
As my studies progressed, I began to appreciate just how difficult that ambition was. Cancer isn’t a single disease, and understanding its biology doesn’t necessarily mean we know how to treat it. Even when researchers make promising discoveries, it can take decades before those discoveries become treatments.
I developed an enormous respect for the patience and persistence that laboratory research demands. At the same time, I began questioning whether this was the kind of work I wanted to pursue. I was still interested in science, but I wasn’t entirely sure where I belonged within it.
That started to change when I joined the Children’s Hospital Research Institute of Manitoba as a research assistant. I’d encountered public health during my undergraduate studies, but most of my training had focused on the biological mechanisms of disease. Working on population health studies introduced me to a different side of medical research. I became interested in how people’s circumstances influence their health and why some communities experience greater difficulties accessing care.
I hadn’t expected to enjoy this kind of research as much as I did.
When COVID-19 arrived, I had the opportunity to work in public health in a different way. I joined the Government of Manitoba as an infectious disease epidemiologist, working alongside professionals involved in the provincial pandemic response.
The work was unlike anything I’d experienced before. We were interpreting data as the situation changed, often without all the information we needed. Decisions couldn’t always wait. Working alongside laboratory teams and medical officers of health, I experienced the urgency of a public health response in a way I hadn’t before.
I was also struck by how much coordination it took. Epidemiologists were only one part of the response. Clinicians and colleagues across government departments had important roles too, and we all depended on one another’s work.
I enjoyed the challenge of working through uncertainty, but what stayed with me most was how quickly our work was being put to use. In academic research, you can spend months on a project, publish the findings and move on without knowing how they’ve influenced practice. During the pandemic, the analyses we were doing were informing decisions as the situation unfolded.
I came away knowing that applied public health was something I wanted to pursue.
Over time, I became increasingly interested in HIV and other sexually transmitted infections.
Having studied molecular biology, I remembered learning about HIV’s formidable reverse transcriptase. It’s one reason the virus can change so quickly, making an effective vaccine particularly difficult to develop. Finding a cure is another challenge because HIV can remain hidden in the body, even with effective treatment. So I began thinking about HIV from a different angle. If a vaccine or cure remained out of reach, what could we do to prevent more people from acquiring it?
We already have effective tools to prevent transmission, and advances in treatment have transformed what it means to live with HIV. But many people still face difficulties accessing these services.
I found myself thinking more about the distance between what science has made possible and what people can realistically access.
My interest in sexual health is also personal. In the conservative Filipino communities I knew growing up, talking openly about sex was taboo. Even asking basic questions about sexual health could be difficult, despite how important those conversations were.
Seeing HIV cases rise in the Philippines, especially among young people, worries me. It makes me think about how much more we could do to make sexual health education accessible. How can you ask a question you don’t even know you need to ask? It bothers me that fear of judgement can still stop people from getting tested. No one should have to feel ashamed of looking after their health.
There’s another part of my childhood that has stayed with me.
When I was seven years old, I knew children my age who were being sexually exploited for money. I remember wanting to play with them, but sometimes they couldn’t, and I didn’t understand why. It was only as I grew older that I began to understand those moments, and how difficult life could be when there wasn’t even enough money for food. I was far too young to fully understand what was happening, but it was already part of the lives of children around me.
While I was able to enjoy being a child, they were facing circumstances no child should have to experience. They deserved so much more than what they had to go through, and they still do.
It’s difficult for me to think about health as a matter of individual choice alone. Not everyone has the same opportunities to look after their health, and I think we need to remember that when we talk about prevention.
At the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, I’ve been able to explore these questions through my research on HIV and STI prevention. I’m particularly interested in how people engage with health services and what can be learned from interventions designed to improve access to care.
My research has also made me more conscious of whose experiences we pay attention to. That can shape the questions we ask and what we learn from them.
I still value the scientific training that first drew me into molecular biology. What has changed is the kinds of questions I want to investigate and the ways I hope to contribute.
Academic research remains important to me, but I also want to make what I learn useful beyond academic publications. Writing has become one way for me to do that. That’s partly why I created this website. It gives me a place to share my research, reflect on what I’m learning and explore questions that I’m still working through.
I once imagined that my contribution to medicine would come from helping discover a cure. I still admire the scientists pursuing those discoveries, and I know how important their work is.
These days, I find myself asking a different question: how can we make better use of the knowledge and interventions we already have so that more people can benefit from them?
I don’t have all the answers. But I know that this is the kind of work I want to keep doing.
–Ayel

title: Let’s Talk About STIs | Ayel L. R. Batac
text:
Let’s Talk About STIs
May 10, 2025
\(~\)
Sexual health is part of looking after ourselves, but it’s not always something people feel comfortable talking about.
Working on HIV and STI prevention has made me think about how much we assume people already know about sexual health. Even knowing when to get tested isn’t necessarily obvious if no one’s explained it.

What are STIs?
STIs, or sexually transmitted infections, are infections that can be passed from one person to another through sexual contact. Depending on the infection, this can happen during vaginal, anal or oral sex. Some can also spread through close skin-to-skin contact.
Certain infections can also spread through exposure to infected blood, such as when needles are shared. Some, including HIV, can also pass from a parent to a baby during pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding.
Some of the most common STIs include:

Chlamydia
Gonorrhoea
Syphilis

Trichomoniasis
Human papillomavirus (HPV)
Genital herpes (herpes simplex virus)
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
Hepatitis B

Hepatitis C can also be transmitted sexually in some circumstances, although it’s more commonly spread through blood.
These infections aren’t all the same. Some, such as chlamydia and syphilis, can usually be cured with antibiotics. Others, including HIV and herpes, can be managed with treatment.


How common are STIs?
According to the World Health Organization ↗, more than one million new infections with four curable STIs (chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and trichomoniasis) occur every day worldwide among people aged 15 to 49.
Many STIs don’t cause noticeable symptoms. You can feel perfectly healthy and still have an infection.


Why does testing matter?
Depending on the infection, leaving an STI untreated can have consequences beyond the initial infection. Some can affect fertility, while others may cause complications during pregnancy. Certain infections, including HPV and hepatitis B, can also increase the risk of developing cancer.
Testing can help identify infections that might otherwise go unnoticed. Many STIs can be treated effectively, and early diagnosis can help prevent complications.
For HIV, getting tested can also be the first step towards treatment. Someone living with HIV who maintains an undetectable viral load, meaning the amount of virus in their blood is too low for standard tests to detect, cannot transmit HIV through sex. This is known as Undetectable = Untransmittable, or U=U.


What sex education meant to me
I received sex education in high school in Canada. We learned about contraception, including condoms and birth control pills, and where to access sexual health services.
I still remember a demonstration involving a condom and a model. There was plenty of nervous laughter in the classroom, as you might expect. But looking back, I appreciate how useful that lesson was.
That was quite different from what I remember of growing up in the Philippines, where conversations about sex were often avoided. Even asking basic questions about sexual health could be difficult, despite how important those conversations were.
That’s one reason I value the sex education I received in Canada. It wasn’t always comfortable, but we were encouraged to ask questions.


Why can getting tested still be difficult?
One thing I’ve learned through my research is that knowing what to do doesn’t always mean someone feels able to do it.
Someone might want to get tested but worry about being recognised at a clinic. They might not know where testing is available or whether they can afford it. For others, fear of judgement can be enough to put off testing altogether.


What can you do?
There are several ways to look after your sexual health, and you don’t need to know everything before taking the first step.

Find out whether STI testing is recommended for you. Testing may be recommended if you have symptoms, a partner has been diagnosed with an STI or you’ve had a possible exposure. Some people also benefit from routine testing even when they feel well. Which tests you need and how often you should get tested depend on your individual circumstances. STI testing might involve a urine sample, a swab or a blood test, depending on the infection. A sexual health clinic can help you work out which tests are appropriate for you and when to get tested after a possible exposure.
Use condoms consistently and correctly. Condoms are one of the most effective ways to reduce the risk of many STIs, including HIV, gonorrhoea and chlamydia. They don’t eliminate all risk, particularly for infections such as genital herpes, which can spread through contact with skin that a condom doesn’t cover.
Know what prevention options are available. Vaccines can prevent HPV and hepatitis B infections. For HIV, pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) can help prevent infection before exposure. If you think you’ve been exposed to HIV, seek medical advice about post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) straight away. It needs to be started as soon as possible, and no later than 72 hours after exposure.
Make space for conversations about sexual health. This might mean asking a healthcare professional a question you’ve been hesitant to raise, or having an honest conversation with a partner. These discussions might feel uncomfortable at first, but they can help people make more informed decisions.

Different approaches will suit different people. What matters is having reliable information and being able to find the support you need.
There’s a difference between being told to use a condom and being shown how. I’m glad we had the opportunity to learn something practical, rather than being expected to figure it out on our own.
–Ayel
\(~\)

title: Anaphylaxis Research | Ayel L. R. Batac
text:
\(~\)
Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction that can develop rapidly and become life-threatening. It may cause breathing difficulties or a sudden drop in blood pressure. Intramuscular adrenaline (also known as epinephrine), administered by injection into a muscle, is the recommended first-line treatment ↗ for anaphylaxis. Despite this established clinical recommendation, adrenaline remains underused in emergency care.
My research examines the gap between recommended anaphylaxis treatment and the care people receive in practice. I am particularly interested in how differences between health systems affect access to emergency treatment and preparedness for anaphylaxis.


Studies across different healthcare settings have documented the underuse of adrenaline during anaphylaxis, with antihistamines or corticosteroids sometimes administered in its place. Antihistamines can relieve certain symptoms of allergic reactions, such as itching and hives, but neither medication can substitute for adrenaline in the emergency treatment of anaphylaxis ↗.
Differences in treatment practices may reflect how healthcare professionals recognise and manage anaphylaxis, as well as the resources available within their healthcare settings. Understanding whether recommended treatments are accessible and appropriately administered is important when examining variation in emergency care.


I am leading an international scoping review examining how anaphylaxis is treated across different healthcare systems. The review maps existing evidence on emergency treatment and examines how reported practices compare with clinical recommendations.
Key areas of investigation include:

Treatment practices: Examining international differences in the use of adrenaline and other medications during anaphylaxis.
Access to treatment: Investigating reported differences in the availability and affordability of adrenaline.
Guideline adherence: Assessing how reported treatment practices align with clinical recommendations.
Barriers to appropriate care: Examining factors that may prevent or delay the administration of adrenaline.

The review considers the circumstances in which treatment practices have been documented, recognising that differences between studies may reflect how treatment is recorded as well as genuine variation in clinical practice.




Adrenaline auto-injectors (AAIs) allow people at risk of anaphylaxis or their caregivers to administer adrenaline before reaching hospital. Early administration is an important part of emergency treatment, but patients may require additional doses of adrenaline ↗ if symptoms persist or recur. Access to subsequent medical assessment and emergency care therefore remains important even when prehospital treatment is available.
AAIs remain unavailable or difficult to obtain in many parts of the world. Where adrenaline is predominantly supplied in ampoules, small sealed containers from which the medication must be drawn into a syringe, patients may depend on trained healthcare professionals to administer their first dose. This can delay treatment when emergency medical assistance is not immediately available.
International disparities in AAI availability ↗ mean that opportunities for prehospital treatment differ considerably between countries. Even where these devices are available, their cost can limit access for people at risk of anaphylaxis.


The regional approval for the import of an adrenaline auto-injector into the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area in 2023 ↗ marked an important development in anaphylaxis management in mainland China, where treatment had traditionally relied on adrenaline administered from ampoules.
In my invited 2025 editorial ↗, I examined the implications of this development for access to emergency treatment. At the time of publication, the availability of AAIs remained geographically restricted, and their substantially higher cost compared with adrenaline ampoules raised concerns about affordability.
The experience in China illustrates why regulatory approval must be accompanied by efforts to make these devices affordable and accessible. Their introduction into routine clinical practice also requires appropriate prescribing and education for people at risk of anaphylaxis.




Improving anaphylaxis outcomes depends in part on whether people can receive appropriate emergency treatment when and where a reaction occurs. By examining international treatment practices and inequalities in adrenaline access, my research aims to contribute to public health by:

Informing medicine access policies that address the affordability and availability of adrenaline, including AAIs.
Supporting improvements in emergency care where treatment practices differ from clinical recommendations.
Informing strategies to improve preparedness for anaphylaxis before patients reach hospital and following discharge.
Identifying geographical gaps in the evidence to guide future anaphylaxis research in underrepresented settings.

title: U=U: What It Means and Why It Matters | Ayel L. R. Batac
text:
U=U: What It Means and Why It Matters
May 23, 2025
\(~\)
One of the things I wish more people understood about HIV is just how much treatment has changed what it means to live with the virus.
Effective HIV treatment doesn’t only help people stay healthy. When someone maintains an undetectable viral load through treatment, they cannot transmit HIV through sex.
This is known as Undetectable = Untransmittable, or U=U.

What does U=U mean?
Antiretroviral therapy (ART) works by preventing HIV from making copies of itself. With effective treatment, the amount of HIV in someone’s blood, known as their viral load, can fall to levels too low for a test to detect.
This is called having an undetectable viral load.
An undetectable viral load doesn’t mean HIV has been cured. The virus remains in the body, and treatment needs to continue to keep it under control.
The evidence for U=U applies when a person’s viral load stays below 200 copies of HIV per mL of blood ↗. This prevents sexual transmission, even if a sensitive test detects a small amount of HIV.
Because viral suppression takes time to achieve, U=U doesn’t apply immediately after someone starts treatment. Regular viral load testing helps confirm when suppression has been achieved and maintained.


How do we know that U=U works?
Three major studies have helped establish what we know about HIV treatment and sexual transmission.

🧪 HPTN 052 (2011 and 2016)
The HPTN 052 study followed more than 1,700 couples where one partner was living with HIV. Nearly all (97%) were heterosexual. Researchers compared starting HIV treatment early with delaying it.
The initial findings published in 2011 ↗ showed that starting treatment earlier reduced the risk of HIV transmission to the partner who wasn’t living with HIV by 96%.
The final results published in 2016 ↗ confirmed the benefits of earlier treatment over longer follow-up. Importantly, no HIV transmissions linked between partners occurred during stable viral suppression.


🧪 PARTNER (2016)
The PARTNER study ↗ examined HIV transmission among heterosexual and gay couples where one partner was living with HIV and taking effective treatment.
The analysis included 888 couples who reported having sex without condoms while the partner living with HIV maintained viral suppression.
There were no HIV transmissions linked between partners during the eligible follow-up period.


🧪 PARTNER2 Study (2019)
The PARTNER2 study ↗ provided further evidence among gay male couples.
During the study, participants reported approximately 76,000 acts of condomless anal sex while the partner living with HIV maintained viral suppression.
Again, researchers found no HIV transmissions linked between partners. Some people who were HIV-negative at the start of the PARTNER studies acquired HIV during follow-up, but genetic testing showed that these infections weren’t linked to their study partners.



What does this mean for people living with HIV?
For a person living with HIV, knowing that effective treatment prevents sexual transmission can change how they think about relationships and intimacy. It can also help address fears that may have been shaped by outdated information about HIV.
Knowing about U=U doesn’t mean that stigma disappears. People’s experiences of HIV are shaped by more than their viral load, and no one should have to demonstrate that they’re undetectable to be treated with dignity.


Access to treatment matters
Achieving and maintaining an undetectable viral load depends on having reliable access to HIV treatment. People also need ongoing care to make sure their treatment continues to work.
That isn’t always straightforward. The cost of treatment can be a barrier in some settings, while others may struggle to attend appointments or access regular viral load testing. Stigma can make seeking HIV care difficult too.


What about other STIs?
U=U refers specifically to the sexual transmission of HIV. It doesn’t prevent other STIs, including gonorrhoea, chlamydia, and syphilis.
Condoms remain an effective way to reduce the risk of many STIs. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) helps people without HIV prevent infection, while vaccines can prevent certain infections, including HPV (human papillomavirus) and hepatitis B.


U=U at a glance

For me, U=U is one of those scientific findings that should be part of an ordinary conversation about HIV care. People shouldn’t have to come across this information by chance.

title: Research | Ayel L. R. Batac
text:
My research focuses on the social epidemiology of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), particularly among marginalized and underserved populations such as men who have sex with men (MSM) and sex worker communities. I am especially interested in how social conditions, health behaviours, and the organization of health services shape access to STI prevention and care. Much of my work examines inequities in testing and how prevention strategies can better reach populations underserved by existing services.
This interest extends to infectious disease prevention in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and other low-resource settings. My current research in China examines whether a pay-it-forward approach can increase gonorrhoea and chlamydia testing among MSM. Through this approach, individuals receive testing as a gift and may choose to contribute toward testing for someone else. This work evaluates an alternative model for expanding access to STI testing while incorporating community participation into service delivery.
Methodologically, I use mixed methods to address questions in epidemiology and health policy while drawing on the social and behavioural sciences to understand engagement with infectious disease prevention and health services. I also use community-based and participatory approaches, including crowdsourcing, to involve communities in developing responses to public health problems. My work in knowledge translation and knowledge mobilization examines how research findings and community-generated knowledge are used in public health decision-making.
My broader work in infectious diseases includes respiratory infections and tropical diseases that contribute substantially to disease burden in LMICs. I am also developing work in health economics and infectious disease modelling. In health economics, my research focuses on the economic evaluation of HIV prevention using pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and STI prevention using doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxyPEP). My interests in infectious disease modelling centre on participatory mathematical modelling and the incorporation of community perspectives into modelling processes.
Alongside my work in infectious diseases, I have maintained a longstanding interest in allergy and clinical immunology, particularly anaphylaxis and allergen immunotherapy.

This interest extends to infectious disease prevention in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and other low-resource settings. My current research in China examines whether a pay-it-forward approach can increase gonorrhoea and chlamydia testing among MSM. Through this approach, individuals receive testing as a gift and may choose to contribute toward testing for someone else. This work evaluates an alternative model for expanding access to STI testing while incorporating community participation into service delivery.
Methodologically, I use mixed methods to address questions in epidemiology and health policy while drawing on the social and behavioural sciences to understand engagement with infectious disease prevention and health services. I also use community-based and participatory approaches, including crowdsourcing, to involve communities in developing responses to public health problems. My work in knowledge translation and knowledge mobilization examines how research findings and community-generated knowledge are used in public health decision-making.
My broader work in infectious diseases includes respiratory infections and tropical diseases that contribute substantially to disease burden in LMICs. I am also developing work in health economics and infectious disease modelling. In health economics, my research focuses on the economic evaluation of HIV prevention using pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and STI prevention using doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxyPEP). My interests in infectious disease modelling centre on participatory mathematical modelling and the incorporation of community perspectives into modelling processes.
Alongside my work in infectious diseases, I have maintained a longstanding interest in allergy and clinical immunology, particularly anaphylaxis and allergen immunotherapy.

title: Syphilis Self-Testing: Rethinking Access to Diagnosis | Ayel L. R. Batac
text:
Syphilis Self-Testing: Rethinking Access to Diagnosis
January 2, 2026
\(~\)
One of the things that concerns me about syphilis is that we already know how to cure it, but infections continue to rise in many parts of the world. The World Health Organization estimates ↗ that the number of new syphilis infections worldwide among adults aged 15 to 49 increased from 7.1 million in 2020 to 8 million in 2022.
Like many sexually transmitted infections, syphilis doesn’t always cause noticeable symptoms ↗. People may have the infection for some time without knowing it. Without testing, the infection can go untreated and potentially be passed on to others.
Having lived in both the Philippines and Canada, I have seen how much getting care can depend on what is available nearby and what someone can afford.
I have continued to explore these issues through my work on infectious disease diagnostics. In 2025, I co-authored a commentary in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology ↗ with Professors Michael Marks ↗, Joseph Tucker ↗, and Rosanna Peeling ↗ on the role of syphilis self-testing in prevention and control.
One of the questions we explored was who might be missing out on testing through conventional diagnostic services.

When testing depends on the clinic
In Canada, getting tested for syphilis often involves visiting a healthcare provider and having a blood sample collected for laboratory testing ↗. The results are then used to determine whether further assessment or treatment is needed.
For many people, this approach works well. But someone who lives several hours away from a clinic might need to take time off work and pay for transport just to get tested, particularly if another appointment is needed. Someone else might live close to a clinic but worry about being recognised there.
Both might benefit from having the option to test somewhere other than a clinic.


What is syphilis self-testing?
Syphilis self-testing allows people to test themselves outside a clinic, including at home. Most self-tests use a small blood sample collected through a finger prick and provide a result within minutes.
In August 2024, the United States Food and Drug Administration authorised the country’s first at-home, over-the-counter syphilis test ↗. The World Health Organization also published recommendations in 2024 ↗ suggesting that self-testing be offered as an additional approach to syphilis testing.


What have we learned from research?
A randomised controlled trial published in 2022 ↗ recruited 451 men who have sex with men (MSM) across 124 cities in China. Participants hadn’t been tested for syphilis in the previous six months. Researchers compared conventional testing services with free dual HIV and syphilis self-tests delivered by post, with or without a lottery-based financial incentive.
Over the six-month study period, approximately 63% of MSM in the self-testing group without the lottery incentive got tested for syphilis, compared with around 15% of those receiving the usual testing services.
What stood out to me was that nearly 80% of those who self-tested reported never having been tested for syphilis before.
The trial took place during the COVID-19 pandemic, when restrictions on clinic-based testing may have increased demand for self-testing.
In Zimbabwe, a randomised controlled trial published in 2023 ↗ recruited 100 participants in Harare through community-based organisations working with MSM. Researchers compared community-based syphilis self-testing with facility-based testing.
Testing uptake was 74% among those offered self-testing and 58% among those referred to a healthcare facility. However, the study didn’t provide enough evidence to establish a difference between the two approaches.
The researchers also found that self-testing cost less per person tested from the service provider’s perspective.
Of the six participants who received a reactive (positive) self-test result, four returned for confirmatory testing. Being able to complete the initial test didn’t guarantee that everyone would receive further testing.


A self-test isn’t the same as a diagnosis
Most syphilis self-tests detect antibodies that the body produces in response to the bacterium that causes syphilis. These antibodies can remain detectable long after an infection has been successfully treated.
A reactive self-test result may indicate a current or previously treated infection. False-positive results are also possible. Further testing and clinical assessment are needed ↗ to determine whether treatment is necessary.
The timing of testing matters too. Someone who has recently acquired syphilis may not yet have developed enough antibodies for the test to detect. If you have symptoms or think you’ve been exposed to syphilis, seek medical advice promptly, even if your self-test result is negative.


Making self-testing work in practice
If self-tests are only available for purchase online or in pharmacies, people who can’t afford them may still be left out. Distributing free or subsidised tests through community-based organisations could help extend their reach.
Some people might want help using the test, while others would prefer to do it on their own.
HIV self-testing has taught us that providing someone with a test kit is only part of the work ↗. Someone who receives a reactive result at home needs to know where to go for further testing. Even if they do, they may encounter the same difficulties that made accessing clinic-based testing challenging in the first place.
We have evidence that self-testing can increase testing uptake. What we still need to understand is whether it helps people get diagnosed and treated sooner.
I don’t see self-testing as a replacement for laboratories or existing sexual health services. It’s another way for people to begin accessing those services.
I would like someone who tests for syphilis at home to have as clear a route to treatment as someone who gets tested at a clinic.
–Ayel

title: Tuberculosis Research | Ayel L. R. Batac
text:
\(~\)
Early detection of tuberculosis (TB) is essential to preventing severe illness and reducing transmission. Yet access to TB screening remains uneven, particularly in remote and underserved communities where healthcare services may have limited capacity.
My research examines how TB screening interventions can be delivered within existing health systems while responding to the needs of the communities they serve. I am particularly interested in the practical demands of community-wide screening and how these interventions function alongside routine healthcare services.


Routine approaches to detecting TB often depend on people seeking care when symptoms develop or being identified through contact tracing. During some outbreaks, these approaches may miss individuals with undetected TB, particularly when symptoms are absent or connections between cases are difficult to establish. Community-wide screening offers a more proactive approach by extending screening to a broader population. It can identify people who require further assessment for TB disease, while screening for TB infection may identify those who could benefit from preventive treatment once active disease has been excluded.
Community-wide screening may be particularly valuable when ongoing transmission suggests that routine testing and contact tracing alone are insufficient. However, delivering screening at this scale can place considerable demands on healthcare services. In remote settings, additional personnel and diagnostic resources may be needed while local facilities continue providing routine care.



TB-related stigma and concerns about confidentiality can discourage people from participating in screening, even when services are available. Practical barriers may also differ between communities, particularly when the location or timing of screening activities makes participation difficult. Involving community members in planning can help public health teams identify these challenges and adapt how screening is delivered.
Local leaders and residents can influence how information about TB is communicated and how screening services are organised. Their involvement is particularly meaningful when communities have opportunities to shape decisions during planning, rather than being consulted only after an intervention has been designed.



People identified through community-wide screening may require further diagnostic assessment, while treatment for TB disease or infection may continue long after a temporary screening clinic closes. Clear referral pathways are essential to connect these individuals with existing TB services and ensure access to appropriate follow-up care. Without sufficient capacity to provide ongoing care, the benefits of expanded screening may be limited.
Screening participation and case detection figures provide only part of the evidence needed to evaluate an intervention. Examining how screening was organised and delivered can reveal challenges that may not be apparent from these outcomes alone. Understanding where difficulties arose can help public health teams identify practical improvements for future screening responses.



Community-wide screening can create opportunities to identify tuberculosis earlier and reach people who might otherwise remain undiagnosed. When supported by appropriate healthcare services, these interventions have the potential to contribute to TB prevention and control by:

Supporting earlier diagnosis and treatment of TB disease, with the potential to reduce further transmission.

Expanding opportunities for preventive treatment among people with TB infection who might otherwise remain unidentified.

Reducing inequities in access to TB screening among populations underserved by conventional healthcare services.

Strengthening public health preparedness by informing more effective and locally responsive approaches to future TB outbreaks.

\(~\)

The clinic reached 89.2% of its original screening target and identified individuals requiring treatment for TB infection or disease. Drawing on findings from an internal After Action Review, the article explores how community engagement and operational experience can inform future screening responses in remote northern settings.

title: Anaphylaxis: Why Access to Adrenaline Matters | Ayel L. R. Batac
text:
Anaphylaxis: Why Access to Adrenaline Matters
March 10, 2026
\(~\)
Adrenaline, also known as epinephrine, is the recommended first treatment for anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction that can quickly become life-threatening. I’m interested in why it can be harder to obtain adrenaline in some places than in others.
Growing up in the Philippines, I was used to seeing nebulisers in homes and clinics. These machines turn liquid medication into a mist that can be inhaled. Salbutamol, a medication used to relieve breathing difficulties associated with asthma, was commonly used and relatively inexpensive where I lived. Once a family had bought a nebuliser, they could reuse the machine and purchase the medication separately as needed.
When I moved to Canada, I noticed how much more common metered-dose inhalers, often called puffers, were. I hadn’t given much thought before to how cost and availability could influence which medications families kept at home.

Access to adrenaline
It’s particularly important for people at risk of anaphylaxis to have adrenaline available before an emergency occurs. Someone experiencing anaphylaxis may need adrenaline before medical help arrives.
During anaphylaxis, the airways can swell and narrow, and blood pressure can fall dangerously low. Adrenaline helps reduce this swelling, improve breathing, and raise blood pressure.
Signs of anaphylaxis can include sudden difficulty breathing, swelling of the throat or tongue, and feeling faint. Some people also develop raised, itchy patches on their skin, known as hives, although anaphylaxis can occur without any skin symptoms.
International guidelines on anaphylaxis management ↗ recommend giving adrenaline promptly by injecting it into the muscle of the outer thigh.
Anaphylaxis is a medical emergency. If anaphylaxis is suspected, administer adrenaline promptly using the person’s recommended emergency device, if available, and call emergency services immediately ↗.
Adrenaline auto-injectors allow people at risk of anaphylaxis to carry the medication with them and administer it without having to prepare an injection themselves. People who have been advised to carry adrenaline auto-injectors should carry two with them, know how to use them and check regularly that they haven’t expired ↗.
Adrenaline may be available in a country even when auto-injectors are not.
In a 2023 survey ↗, the World Allergy Organization received responses from members in 66 countries. Adrenaline auto-injectors were reported to be available in only 60% of the countries surveyed. In some countries, people had to rely on importing the devices themselves.
In 2025, I wrote an editorial in Clinical & Experimental Allergy ↗ examining the introduction of adrenaline auto-injectors in mainland China.
Adrenaline auto-injectors were approved for clinical use in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area in 2023. At the time I wrote the editorial, their availability elsewhere in mainland China remained limited.
Before auto-injectors were introduced in the region, adrenaline was commonly given using a syringe. The medication had to be drawn from an ampoule, a small sealed container, and prepared for injection. This generally required a trained healthcare professional.
Even where these devices are available, the cost of obtaining and replacing them can make it difficult for some families to keep adrenaline on hand.


Why treatment can differ from guidelines
The availability of adrenaline is only one part of anaphylaxis management. Recognising anaphylaxis and knowing when to administer the medication are also important.
A study published in 2020 ↗ reviewed medical reports describing 819 cases of anaphylaxis in China. The reports were published between 2014 and 2018. Adrenaline was the first medication given in approximately 39% of cases, while corticosteroids, which are medications used to reduce inflammation, were given first in approximately 44%.
More than two-thirds of the episodes occurred in people who were already in hospital, and almost all involved severe reactions. These cases don’t necessarily reflect how anaphylaxis was managed across China, but they show that treatment didn’t always follow international recommendations.
Antihistamines can help relieve itching and hives once the life-threatening symptoms have been addressed, while salbutamol can help relieve wheezing. Corticosteroids are no longer recommended for routine emergency treatment of anaphylaxis under current UK resuscitation guidance ↗. None of these medications should replace or delay adrenaline.
It’s easy to describe differences in treatment as a failure to follow guidelines. I’m interested in understanding what might explain those differences.
In some settings, healthcare professionals may have limited access to particular medications or devices. In others, they may have difficulty recognising anaphylaxis or may not have enough training to respond to it promptly.
For people at risk of anaphylaxis, being prescribed adrenaline doesn’t necessarily mean they can afford to obtain it or feel confident using it.


Adrenaline without an injection
Until recently, people who needed to administer adrenaline themselves generally relied on injectable devices.
In August 2024, the United States Food and Drug Administration approved neffy ↗, an adrenaline nasal spray for the emergency treatment of severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis.
The nasal spray was also authorised in the United Kingdom in July 2025 ↗ under the name EURneffy.
The manufacturer applied for approval in Canada in January 2025 ↗, although the nasal spray has not yet been authorised.
For someone who is afraid of needles, having the option to administer adrenaline through a nasal spray may make treatment feel less intimidating.
In a manufacturer-sponsored study published in 2023 ↗, researchers compared nasal adrenaline with two methods of injecting adrenaline in 59 healthy volunteers. On average, the highest level of adrenaline reached in the bloodstream after using the nasal spray fell between the levels reached with the two injection methods.
The researchers also examined changes in blood pressure and heart rate. Both increased after nasal or injectable adrenaline was given, although the effects varied. However, the participants weren’t experiencing anaphylaxis, so the study can’t tell us whether nasal and injectable adrenaline work equally well during an emergency.
A small, manufacturer-sponsored study published in 2025 ↗ examined nasal adrenaline in 15 children and adolescents who experienced moderate anaphylaxis during supervised food challenges.
Food challenges ↗ involve giving someone small, gradually increasing amounts of a food under medical supervision to determine whether they’re allergic to it. Although the reactions in this study were classified as moderate, they still required prompt treatment with adrenaline.
None of the participants required a second dose of adrenaline to treat the initial reaction. One participant’s symptoms returned nearly three hours later, and they were given an adrenaline injection.
The study didn’t directly compare nasal adrenaline with injectable adrenaline. We also don’t know whether the results would be the same if someone had to recognise and treat anaphylaxis themselves at home.
I’m also interested in what happens after a new treatment is authorised. Will people who struggle with injectable adrenaline be able to obtain the nasal spray? Will it be affordable enough for them to carry and replace when necessary?


Understanding variation in anaphylaxis treatment
Earlier this month, my colleagues in Canada and Australia and I published a scoping review protocol in Clinical & Experimental Allergy ↗.
A scoping review allows us to bring together existing research on a particular subject and identify areas where evidence is still limited. The protocol sets out how we plan to conduct the review.
We want to understand how adrenaline is being used in practice, how treatment differs across healthcare settings and what might explain those differences.
When someone at risk of anaphylaxis is advised to carry adrenaline, I would like them to be able to obtain it and feel confident using it when they need it.
–Ayel

Partner, National Collaborating Centre for Infectious Diseases, Rady Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Manitoba







I am a public health scientist interested in how people perceive health risks and make decisions about prevention and care. My research draws on the social and behavioural sciences and epidemiology, using mixed methods to investigate how people experience healthcare and how health systems respond to their needs. As an implementation scientist, I am interested not only in whether an intervention works, but in how it works, for whom and under what conditions.
In China, I am evaluating behavioural interventions designed to increase sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing among men who have sex with men (MSM). My research in the United Kingdom and Australia examines perceptions of the potential use of the four-component meningococcal serogroup B (4CMenB) vaccine for gonorrhoea prevention. I also investigate how decentralised STI diagnostics, particularly syphilis self-testing, can expand access while connecting people who test positive with further testing and treatment. Community engagement helps identify how stigma and other barriers affect access to testing among sexual minorities and sex workers. Beyond sexual health, I lead international research on access to anaphylaxis treatment and emergency care preparedness, where similar questions about service availability and timely care arise.
My earlier research in allergy and clinical immunology examined the psychosocial and economic burden of paediatric food allergy and how concerns about allergic reactions shaped confidence in COVID-19 vaccination. My work in maternal and child health also explored how chronic childhood illness affects family relationships. These experiences continue to inform my mixed methods approach, particularly my interest in understanding health outcomes alongside the experiences of those affected.
In low-resource settings, I use participatory research approaches to identify social innovations developed by communities in response to unmet health needs. Crowdsourcing allows me to draw on collective intelligence and bring attention to locally developed solutions that might otherwise go unrecognised. Through co-creation, I work with communities to understand how these innovations operate in practice. I believe that solutions emerging from resource-constrained settings deserve greater recognition, both for their role in addressing local health needs and for what others can learn from the experiences behind them.
I value research conducted with, rather than simply about, the communities and public health partners connected to the issues being studied. Their knowledge and experiences can help shape research questions and ensure that findings remain relevant to the challenges they encounter in practice. For me, knowledge translation begins during the research process through ongoing collaboration with those who can help interpret findings and put them to use in public health practice. Ultimately, I want my research to remain accountable to the people and communities whose health and care it seeks to improve.

title: Sexually Transmitted Infections Research | Ayel L. R. Batac
text:
\(~\)
Sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including gonorrhoea and chlamydia, remain a significant public health concern worldwide. Many STIs cause few or no symptoms and may go undiagnosed without timely testing. In many settings, men who have sex with men (MSM) experience a disproportionate burden of STIs, making regular access to testing particularly important. Stigma surrounding same-sex sexual behaviour and concerns about confidentiality can discourage engagement with STI services. Out-of-pocket costs may create further barriers, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where affordable testing is not consistently available.
My research examines how social and behavioural factors shape people’s engagement with STI prevention and their experiences of sexual health services. Using mixed methods, I investigate these relationships and consider how the evidence can inform the design and implementation of public health interventions.



  

    
    
      Focus 01
      
        Pay-It-Forward STI Testing
      
      
        Social innovation in STI testing.
      
    

    
    
      Focus 02
      
        Vaccination for STI Prevention
      
      
        Evolving perspectives on gonorrhoea vaccination.
      
    

  






The pay-it-forward strategy is a social innovation built on a simple idea: people can receive a health service free of charge and, if they wish, help someone else access the same service. In STI testing, this means offering free gonorrhoea and chlamydia tests while inviting recipients to contribute towards testing for others. Participation is entirely voluntary, and access to testing does not depend on making a contribution.
The approach reduces the immediate cost of testing while creating opportunities for people to support others who may face similar barriers to care:

Access: Reducing financial barriers to STI testing.
Reciprocity: Encouraging voluntary contributions that help others access testing.
Community participation: Creating opportunities for individuals to support STI prevention by recommending testing to peers.

Unlike conventional fee-for-service models, pay-it-forward introduces community support into the delivery of healthcare. The strategy may be particularly relevant in settings where financial constraints limit access to STI services, although stigma and concerns about confidentiality may still discourage people from seeking care.



STI testing programmes often measure their reach through the number of people who access services. Pay-it-forward introduces another dimension of participation, allowing individuals to contribute to the health of others rather than remaining solely recipients of care. This creates opportunities for communities to take a more active role in STI prevention, particularly through the social networks and relationships that connect people beyond conventional healthcare settings.
Meaningful participation, however, may take different forms depending on people’s circumstances. Individuals who wish to support others may still be reluctant to engage in activities that could reveal their sexual health concerns or expose them to stigma. Recognising these differences can help public health programmes create opportunities for community involvement that respect individual preferences and allow people to contribute in ways they feel comfortable.



A pragmatic cluster randomised controlled trial (RCT) conducted through community-based organisations and public health clinics in Guangdong Province, China, provides the basis for my ongoing mixed methods research on pay-it-forward gonorrhoea and chlamydia testing among MSM. The work examines the effectiveness and implementation of the strategy, with particular attention to how individuals engage with opportunities to support others.
Survey data provide information about patterns of participation, while qualitative interviews explore what motivates individuals to contribute and what may discourage them from doing so. The research focuses on:

STI testing uptake: Evaluating how pay-it-forward strategies influence the use of gonorrhoea and chlamydia testing services.
Prosocial behaviour and community participation: Investigating motivations for voluntary contributions and how community connectedness may shape engagement with the intervention.
Stigma and participation: Examining how concerns about others discovering an individual’s use of STI services or same-sex sexual behaviour may influence their willingness to participate.

Understanding these experiences can inform how pay-it-forward is delivered within existing sexual health services, particularly by accommodating different forms of participation while respecting privacy and individual choice.
Back to Research Foci






The four-component meningococcal serogroup B (4CMenB) vaccine was originally developed to prevent meningococcal disease, a serious bacterial infection that can cause meningitis (inflammation of the lining around the brain and spinal cord) or bloodstream infections. The bacterium responsible for meningococcal disease is closely related to the one that causes gonorrhoea, an STI. Because these bacteria share certain proteins, researchers began investigating whether meningococcal B vaccines might also provide protection against gonorrhoea. Earlier studies found lower rates of gonorrhoea among people who had received these vaccines, suggesting possible partial protection, although the findings did not establish that vaccination itself caused the difference.
In August 2025, England introduced a targeted 4CMenB vaccination programme ↗, primarily for MSM at increased risk of gonorrhoea, including those with a recent bacterial STI diagnosis or multiple recent sexual partners. The decision followed concerns about high gonorrhoea rates and growing antibiotic resistance, alongside evidence suggesting that even partial vaccine protection could have public health benefits. However, more recent clinical trials have not confirmed the protection suggested by earlier studies, leaving uncertainty about the vaccine’s effectiveness against gonorrhoea. Understanding how people interpret this evolving evidence is therefore important for communicating the potential benefits and limitations of vaccination as an STI prevention strategy.



My research examines how vaccination for gonorrhoea prevention is discussed in online communities, with particular attention to how people interpret emerging evidence and express attitudes towards its potential use in STI prevention.
The research uses a mixed methods approach to content analysis, focusing on:

Information needs and attitudes: Examining the questions people raise about vaccination and how they interpret its potential benefits and risks.
Vaccination experiences and access: Exploring reported experiences of obtaining vaccination and the barriers that may influence access.
Changes over time: Investigating how topics and expressed attitudes evolve alongside developments in scientific evidence and vaccination policy.

Understanding these perspectives may help identify gaps in public knowledge and inform how emerging STI prevention strategies are communicated. Findings will reflect the contributions analysed within these online communities rather than being treated as representative of wider population attitudes.
Back to Research Foci




Making STI prevention services available does not guarantee that people will use them. Understanding how individuals engage with testing and respond to emerging preventive approaches can help inform public health practice. My research aims to contribute by:

Supporting earlier STI detection: Informing testing approaches that could improve access to timely diagnosis and treatment, particularly where financial barriers discourage testing.

Strengthening community participation: Helping sexual health services accommodate voluntary contributions while respecting privacy and avoiding pressure to participate.

Improving communication about STI vaccination: Identifying questions and concerns that public health messaging should address, particularly when evidence about vaccine effectiveness remains uncertain.
Informing implementation in practice: Providing evidence about the social and practical considerations that may influence how STI prevention interventions are introduced and delivered within existing health services.

\(~\)
Stay tuned – publications and data visualisations related to this work will be made available here soon.
\(~\)
 This work is conducted in my capacity as a researcher at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine ↗ and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill ↗.

title: neffy in Canada: Same Epinephrine. New Delivery Option. | Ayel L. R. Batac
text:
neffy in Canada: Same Epinephrine. New Delivery Option.
May 15, 2026

 TL;DR 


neffy® is a 2 mg epinephrine nasal spray authorized in Canada for emergency treatment of allergic reactions in people who weigh 30 kg or more.


Epinephrine remains the first-line emergency treatment for anaphylaxis.


neffy does not prevent allergic reactions; after epinephrine is used, people should call 911 or contact local emergency services.


Drug-level and body-response studies support neffy as an emergency epinephrine delivery option, but real-world use during actual anaphylaxis events still needs to be studied.


A new delivery option only helps if people know when to use it, how to use it, and what to do afterward.



What changes when the medication is the same, but the way it’s delivered changes?
That is the question I keep coming back to as neffy becomes available in Canada.
neffy is still epinephrine. It’s still used for emergency treatment of severe allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis. The difference is how it’s given: instead of being injected into the thigh, it’s sprayed into one nostril.
Health Canada has authorized neffy for emergency treatment of allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, in adults and children who weigh 30 kg or more. These reactions may be triggered by insect stings or bites, foods, medications, or other allergens. They may also be idiopathic or exercise-induced. Health Canada has not authorized neffy for patients under 30 kg.
But this is not just a story about a new product. It’s also about whether people are prepared to use it correctly when an emergency happens.

What neffy is, and what it is not
neffy is a needle-free epinephrine nasal spray for emergencies. It’s not an allergy cure. It doesn’t prevent allergic reactions. It doesn’t replace allergen avoidance, an anaphylaxis emergency plan, or the need to contact emergency services after epinephrine is used.
According to the Canadian product monograph, the recommended dose is one spray, containing 2 mg of epinephrine, into one nostril. If symptoms do not improve or symptoms worsen after the first dose, a second dose may be given in the same nostril using a new nasal spray, starting five minutes after the first dose. The product monograph also recommends that patients have immediate access to two neffy nasal sprays at all times.
A nasal spray may seem simple. Anaphylaxis is not.
In an emergency, symptoms can progress quickly. People may panic, hesitate, or second-guess what they are seeing. So even though neffy may look more familiar than an injectable device, it is still epinephrine for a potentially life-threatening situation.
For some people, neffy may be a welcome alternative to an auto-injector. For others, the best option will depend on their clinical history, preferences, access, and emergency plan.


Why the device matters
On paper, neffy is still epinephrine. In real life, the device matters.
A person may know they are supposed to use epinephrine and still hesitate. They may be afraid of needles. A parent or caregiver may worry about using an injectable device incorrectly. Someone nearby may not be sure whether the symptoms are “bad enough”. In the middle of an emergency, even a simple set of instructions can feel harder to follow.
That is one reason neffy is important. A needle-free option may feel less intimidating for some patients, caregivers, teachers, or bystanders. It may also be easier to explain in certain community settings.
But a different device also means different training. It’s not enough to ask whether someone “carries epinephrine”. We need to know which device they carry, where it’s kept, who knows how to use it, and who will call emergency services afterward.


What the evidence shows so far
The question is not whether epinephrine has a role in anaphylaxis. It does. Epinephrine is already the first-line emergency treatment.
The more specific question for neffy is whether a nasal spray can deliver epinephrine into the body in a way that supports emergency use.
Health Canada’s product monograph states that controlled clinical trials for the treatment of anaphylaxis have not been performed with epinephrine. It also states that after one 2 mg nasal dose of neffy, epinephrine levels in the body were generally within the range seen after an epinephrine injection into the muscle over 60 minutes.
Published neffy studies provide supportive evidence about how the medication moves through the body and affects the body after use. In a repeat-dosing study, neffy produced epinephrine levels and physiologic responses within a comparable range to intramuscular epinephrine, including in people with allergy-related nasal symptoms. The same study also supported repeat dosing in the same nostril.
These studies mainly tell us what happens to epinephrine levels in the body after neffy is used. They help answer whether the medication reaches the body. They don’t prove that neffy will improve real-world emergency outcomes compared with existing epinephrine devices. They also don’t tell us whether every person will carry it consistently, recognize anaphylaxis quickly, or use it correctly under stress.
Broader research on intranasal adrenaline supports the scientific plausibility of nasal delivery, but not all of that evidence is specific to neffy. A recent review concluded that clinical efficacy data remain limited, and that long-term real-world evidence on effectiveness and adherence in community settings is still needed.
Based on the evidence so far, neffy appears to be a reasonable emergency epinephrine option for eligible patients. But it still needs to be paired with training, clear instructions, and follow-up in real-world settings.


What Canadians should consider next
For Canadians considering neffy, there are three practical details to sort out.
First, check eligibility. neffy 2 mg is authorized in Canada for people who weigh 30 kg or more. The 1 mg dose for children under 30 kg is not available in Canada at this time.
Second, ask about cost and availability. Food Allergy Canada has reported that neffy is expected to be available in Canadian pharmacies starting in summer 2026. The price will depend on coverage and reimbursement arrangements with provinces and insurance companies.
Third, update the emergency plan around the actual device. If someone carries neffy, the plan should name neffy specifically. It should say that it’s a single-use nasal spray, that a second dose may be given in the same nostril with a new device after five minutes if symptoms do not improve or worsen, and that 911 or local emergency services should be called after epinephrine is used.
The device should be named in the plan, not just the medication.
Patients and families don’t need to make this decision alone. An allergist, primary care provider, or pharmacist can help determine whether neffy fits their allergy history, daily life, and emergency plan.
As neffy becomes available in Canada, access is only part of the story. What matters most is whether the people closest to an allergic emergency are ready to recognize it, use the device, and act without hesitation.
-Ayel

title: Manitoba’s HIV Emergency: When Evidence Doesn’t Reach People | Ayel L. R. Batac
text:
Manitoba’s HIV Emergency: When Evidence Doesn’t Reach People
May 9, 2026

 TL;DR 


Manitoba has declared a public health emergency in response to rising HIV cases.


HIV is preventable and treatable. People living with HIV who are on effective treatment can live long, healthy lives and cannot sexually transmit HIV when they are virally suppressed.


Manitoba already has important HIV prevention and care tools in place.


The challenge is whether people can reach those tools early enough and in ways that keep them connected to care.


This emergency is a systems warning: prevention and treatment only work when care is reachable, trusted, and possible to return to.



Manitoba’s HIV emergency is hard to sit with because HIV is not a mystery anymore.
We know how to prevent HIV. We know how to treat HIV. And still, cases are rising.
On May 7, 2026, Manitoba declared a public health emergency in response to rising HIV cases. New diagnoses increased from 90 in 2019 to 328 in 2025. In 2024, Manitoba’s HIV diagnosis rate was more than three-and-a-half times the national rate. The burden isn’t evenly distributed across the province: diagnosis rates are highest in Prairie Mountain Health and Northern Health, while Winnipeg has the largest number of diagnoses.
I’m from Winnipeg, so this feels close to home. And because I first lived in the Philippines before moving to Canada, I’m careful about the word “access”.
Living across two health system contexts taught me that a service can exist on paper and still be difficult to reach in real life. Access is not simply the presence of a program. It’s whether the path to that program is realistic for the person who needs it.
In the Philippines, I saw how a clinic visit could become difficult once cost, transportation, and uncertainty about the health system entered the picture. In Canada, the barriers may look different, but the core question is familiar: can people actually reach the care that public health tells them is available?
That’s why I don’t read Manitoba’s HIV emergency as a failure of HIV science. The science is strong. The harder question is whether people can reach the tools we already have early enough and in ways that make it possible to stay connected to care.

HIV has changed, but stigma still gets in the way
For many people, HIV is still surrounded by fear, shame, and outdated assumptions. But HIV prevention and treatment have changed dramatically.
A person living with HIV who takes treatment and maintains viral suppression cannot sexually transmit HIV. The Public Health Agency of Canada describes viral suppression as a viral load of less than 200 copies of virus per millilitre of blood, usually measured regularly as part of clinical care.
Stigma is not just a social issue. It follows people into the very moments when they are deciding whether care feels safe enough to seek. If public communication around an HIV emergency increases fear without increasing understanding, it can make the response harder.
The message needs to be clear: HIV is preventable and treatable, and people living with HIV deserve care without shame.


A program existing is not enough
Manitoba is not starting from nothing.
The province has already invested in HIV prevention and care. Through the Manitoba Enhanced Pharmacare Program, key HIV prevention and treatment medications are available at no cost. Manitoba has also supported care models that work closer to the communities most affected, including the Program to Access Treatment for HIV and Support (PATHS).
That work matters. People across the province have been working on HIV prevention and care for years, often in difficult conditions and with communities that have already experienced too much stigma. The emergency declaration should build on that work, not erase it. It should help Manitoba move faster and be more honest about where people are still being missed.
Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is medication that HIV-negative people can take before exposure to prevent HIV. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) can prevent HIV after a possible exposure, but only if it’s started quickly, within 72 hours. Treatment is also prevention. When people living with HIV are diagnosed early and supported to stay on medication, they can live long and healthy lives. When they are virally suppressed, they also cannot sexually transmit HIV.
These tools only work when people can actually use them. Even strong prevention and treatment options lose impact when people encounter them too late, never hear about them, or cannot stay connected to care.
The issue is not that we lack tools. It is that too many people still meet the system too late, or not at all. It is not enough to know that something works. We have to ask whether it works for the people who need it most, in the places where they actually live and seek care.


Why harm reduction belongs in the HIV response
Public health messaging often tells people how to protect themselves from HIV. Those messages matter, but they become incomplete when they are separated from people’s real lives.
Manitoba’s HIV context makes this especially clear. The province has identified both sexual and injection-related transmission as important parts of the current picture. It has also recognized that HIV risk is shaped by the conditions around people’s lives, especially when instability, stigma, substance use, and mistrust of healthcare overlap.
That means harm reduction is not separate from HIV prevention. It is HIV prevention.
In plain language, harm reduction means meeting people where they are. It makes care safer to approach, reduces the risk of infection, and creates a path into testing and treatment without requiring people to be perfect before they are helped.
A person may understand that testing is important and still avoid care because they have been judged before. Someone may want PrEP but have no regular provider to ask. Someone may start HIV treatment and still struggle to stay connected because life is unstable or because healthcare has not always felt safe.
When this happens again and again, it is not just about individual choices. It tells us something about the system people are trying to navigate.


When evidence does not reach people
This access problem is not unique to Manitoba. Around the world, HIV cases can rise even when effective prevention and treatment tools already exist.
The problem is not always that we do not know what to do. Often, the problem is that care does not reach people in time, or in a way they can trust.
In the Philippines, where I grew up for part of my life, UNAIDS has described the country as experiencing the fastest-growing HIV epidemic in the Asia-Pacific region. Estimated new HIV infections increased by 543% from 2010 to 2023, and 33% of new infections occurred among youth aged 15 to 24.
Fiji offers another example of the same implementation challenge. The Government of Fiji declared an HIV outbreak in January 2025 after a sharp increase in newly diagnosed cases. UNAIDS emphasized that the response needed to be stigma-free, community-led, and grounded in both prevention and harm reduction..
I’m not saying Manitoba is the same as the Philippines or Fiji. The contexts are very different. But the lesson is familiar: evidence alone is not enough if systems do not help people use it.


After the declaration
A public health emergency declaration matters. It can focus attention and make it possible to move faster. But the real test begins after the announcement.
For Manitoba, the next step is not simply to tell people that the tools exist. The next step is to make care easier to use when people need it.
HIV testing should feel routine rather than shameful. PrEP conversations should happen before someone has to know the right words to ask. PEP needs to be reachable quickly, including after regular clinic hours. HIV treatment programs need to be flexible enough to keep people connected when daily life is unstable.
Harm reduction, Indigenous-led services, and community-led care should not be treated as add-ons. They are part of the infrastructure of an effective HIV response.
Healthcare providers can also reframe what a missed appointment means. Sometimes it’s not “non-adherence”. Sometimes it’s a sign that the model of care is not flexible enough for the person’s life.
For the broader public, the task is different: replace fear with facts. HIV is not spread through casual contact. People living with HIV are not a threat to their communities.


The bottom line
Manitoba’s HIV emergency should not be read as a failure of individual morality or a failure of biomedical knowledge. It is better understood as a systems warning.
The tools are already here. The challenge is making sure they reach people before the moment to intervene is lost.
That is what access means. It’s not just having a program listed on a website. It’s whether care feels possible to seek and safe enough to return to when life gets complicated.
Access is not a soft issue or a secondary concern. In Manitoba’s HIV emergency, it is what will determine whether prevention and treatment work in real life.
-Ayel
